claims.claim: Hobb proposes a test in which the reader of a passage of dialogue should be able to tell who is speaking without the attribution tags.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: able to tell who is talking without all the little clues

claims.claim: Hobb says that what an assassin notices on entering a room differs from what a child entering the same room notices.
claims.source: Robin Hobb, speaking on Writing Excuses 11.Bonus-01 (Oct 2016), fan transcript at wetranscripts
claims.quote: if you are an assassin and you walk into the room

claims.claim: Hobb says the biographical details filled in around a character build the world at the same time.

claims.quote: details that fill in around the character build the world

claims.claim: Elliott describes the first paragraph of Assassin's Apprentice as an excerpt from a piece being composed inside the story's own world.

claims.quote: the piecing-together of disparate and not always complete sources

verdicts.trueWording: you should be able to tell who is talking without all the little clues like Joe said and Samantha replied
verdicts.note: Robin Hobb, verbatim in the transcript: 'If you want to do a double check, read your dialogue... you should be able to tell who is talking without all the little clues like Joe said and Samantha replied. If you can't tell who's speaking, then maybe you need to do some tweaking on it.' The 'little clues like Joe said and Samantha replied' are exactly the attribution tags, and 'do a double check' is the test framing. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: if you are an assassin and you walk into the room and there's three people there, what he notices is going to be very different from the child character who runs in the room
verdicts.note: Spoken by [Robin] verbatim: '...what he notices is going to be very different from the child character who runs in the room and is totally fixed on finding the toy they left there earlier and the big people standing around talking don't matter at all.' Same room, differing notice - fully supported.

verdicts.trueWording: All of these details that fill in around the character build the world at the same time
verdicts.note: Spoken by [Robin] verbatim, and the enumerated details immediately preceding are biographical: 'What sort of a family did you grow up in? What did your father and your mother do for a living? Are you in a small town? ... Are you wealthy? Are you poor?' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Its first paragraph is an excerpt from a piece being composed within the milieu, not unlike the Encyclopedia Galactica from Asimov's Foundation novels
verdicts.note: Elliott, of Assassin's Apprentice: 'The text of the novel opens with a chapter titled "The Earliest History." Its first paragraph is an excerpt from a piece being composed within the milieu...' Quote verbatim; 'within the milieu' = inside the story's own world.

verdicts.trueWording: I've noted before the Asimovian move of grounding chapters in in-milieu reference materials, something I appreciate
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the commentary paragraph of Entry 226 (Fool's Errand, Chapter 6): 'I am taken by the reminiscence with which the chapter opens. I've noted before the Asimovian move of grounding chapters in in-milieu reference materials...' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: the opening passage is particularly compelling, the piecing-together of disparate and not always complete sources being something with which, as a medievalist, I am familiar
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the same commentary paragraph, and the medievalist limb is Elliott's own words in the same sentence. The chapter opens with Fitz's 'efforts at creating a coherent history of his nation', so the passage does enact the piecing-together.

verdicts.trueWording: it takes it from the mythic realm and fleshes it out with motivations and characters and consequences until it looks like an entirely realistic plot point
verdicts.note: Review body: the big moment is 'lifted straight out of the fairy tale/epic fantasy Big Book of Cliches... What it is is, in a way, a deconstruction of the myth: it takes it from the mythic realm and fleshes it out...' Cliched-plot-point, fleshing-out, and realistic-result limbs all supported.

verdicts.trueWording: it gives us a standard heroic plot, but it tells the story from an unexpected, peripheral perspective, and in the process gives us, as it were, the realistic inner workings of the myth
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the review body, one sentence carrying every limb of the claim.

verdicts.trueWording: Most epic fantasy doesn't spend pages musing on the potential hurt feelings of unsympathetic former lovers or worrying about the apprentice fees for dependants
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Originality: 4/5 paragraph, exactly as the claim's page hint says. The 'most epic fantasy does not spend pages on' limb is the same sentence's subject.

verdicts.trueWording: This is the sort of book that's determined to remind us ... that motivations are personal, and that consequences will also be personal
verdicts.note: Verbatim, closing the Originality: 4/5 paragraph. 'determined to remind us' carries the claim's 'insists'.

verdicts.trueWording: determined to remind us that the fantasy only matters because of the reality in its shadow
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the Originality: 4/5 paragraph; 'remind us' is the reviewer's own verb, matching the claim's 'reminds the reader'.

verdicts.trueWording: So much can be accomplished with only glances
verdicts.note: Review body, and the tenseness limb is supported by the same paragraph's opening: 'It's also a surprisingly tense and exciting book... some of my favourites are the scenes where Fitz is watching the expressions of various characters in a room as they each watch the expressions of the others (and of Fitz).'

verdicts.trueWording: As is usually the case with Hobb, her prose is unremarkable, and the flashes of beautiful imagery are balanced by her willingness to describe the horrific and the ugly
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim in the 'Beauty: 3/5' paragraph, so the 'usually unremarkable' limb is solid. But the reviewer never says where her effect IS located; the sentence continues only about imagery balanced against the horrific and the ugly. The second limb is the analyst's gloss, not the page's statement.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: locating her effect elsewhere than in sentence beauty

verdicts.trueWording: As always, Hobb's prose is solid and effective and occasionally pretty, but isn't going to win awards for its beauty
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the 'Beauty: 3/5' paragraph of the Fool's Fate review; both limbs (solid/effective/occasionally pretty, and not award-winning for beauty) are in the one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: while the language does have that slightly heavy and old-fashioned tone common to the genre, that doesn't prevent it from delivering fantastic lines
verdicts.note: Verbatim in the 'Overall: 7/7. BRILLIANT.' paragraph of the Fool's Quest review, exactly where the claim's page hint places it.
